Method

Source: vignettes/articles/method.Rmd
method.Rmd

This page summarises the method. The derivation and its checks are in the report of the project the package grew out of (to be published).

Why this method

Areal models in space and time attach a latent value to every area-time cell, but surveys usually reach only a small fraction of the cells. The standard tools treat the empty cells in one of two ways. Each makes one of two operations on a Gaussian vector cheap and the other expensive:

  • Marginalising, integrating some cells out, is free when the model is specified by its covariance: the observed cells’ covariance is just their rows and columns. This is how Gaussian-process (geostatistical) models work. They carry only the observed locations, and they predict the rest afterwards by kriging. Conditioning, the rest given the observed, then needs dense matrix solves.
  • Areal priors (CAR, Leroux, BYM, AR1 and random walks in time) are usually specified by their sparse precision matrix, a Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF). Here conditioning is cheap, needing only sparse blocks of the precision. Marginalising destroys the sparsity: the precision of the observed cells alone is a dense Schur complement. GMRF-based software (INLA, Rue et al. 2009; CARBayes, Lee 2013; ICAR models in Stan, Morris et al. 2019) therefore keeps a latent value for every cell, empty or not, because that is what keeps the algebra sparse.

With hundreds of areas and a few decades of months, the full table holds tens of thousands of cells. That is a heavy load for MCMC, and coarser time steps are often chosen to keep it down. stareal takes the Gaussian-process route for areal models. For a separable space-time prior, the covariance between any two cells is the product of a small spatial and a small temporal matrix. The observed cells’ covariance is therefore cheap, as for a Gaussian process, while the areal prior is kept. The model is fitted on the observed cells alone, and the full surface is rebuilt afterwards, one posterior draw at a time.

This pays off when the data are sparse relative to the space-time grid: fine time steps, many areas, few surveys, as is typical of molecular surveillance. It does not when most cells are observed, when the prior is not separable (for example, temporal correlation that varies by area), or when there are tens of thousands of areas.

The model

Space is a set of m areal units (districts, counties, grid cells) with an adjacency graph; time is a regular grid of T steps (months, quarters, years). An area-time cell is one area in one time step. Surveys report y positives out of k tested. For each observed cell,

y_{at} \sim \text{Binomial}\big(k_{at},\ \text{logit}^{-1}(x_{at})\big), \qquad x_{at} = z_{at}^\top \beta + f_{at} + \epsilon_{at}.

  • z_{at}^\top \beta are the fixed effects: an intercept, by default a linear trend in time (trend(), from -1 at the first step to 1 at the last), and any covariates, which may vary by area, by time or by both. Their prior is Gaussian, \beta \sim N(b_0, B).
  • f is a Gaussian field with separable covariance \Sigma = \Sigma_t \otimes \Sigma_s:
    • in space, a Leroux conditional autoregressive model on the graph, with precision Q_s = \tau\{\rho_s R + (1 - \rho_s) I\}, where R = D - W is the graph Laplacian (W the adjacency matrix, D the numbers of neighbours), \sigma^2 = 1/\tau sets the scale and \rho_s \in (0, 1) the strength of spatial dependence;
    • in time, a first-order autoregression with unit variance and lag-one correlation \rho_t.
  • \epsilon_{at} \sim N(0, \sigma_n^2) is a cell-level nugget: variation between surveys that the smooth field does not explain. It applies to the observed cells; the predicted surface is the field without it.

Surveys in the same cell are pooled into one count, y_{at} of k_{at}. This rests on an assumption: given the cell’s latent value x_{at} (nugget included), the surveys in it are independent binomial samples of one prevalence. A sum of independent binomial counts with a common probability is binomial, so under that assumption pooling loses nothing. The model has no variation between surveys within a cell. Two surveys of different sites in the same district and month are treated as one larger survey. If they differ by more than binomial sampling, through different sites, populations or methods, pooling overstates how much the cell’s data say. Longer time steps and larger areas put more surveys together, and make this more likely.

The hyperparameters \theta = (\sigma, \rho_s, \rho_t, \sigma_n) have half-normal and Beta priors (areal_priors()).

Fitting on the observed cells only

Most area-time cells have no data: in the crt K76T tutorial, 264 of 74,304 unit-months. Because everything except the likelihood is Gaussian, the unobserved cells can be integrated out exactly: the n observed cells’ latent values x_o have the Gaussian prior

x_o \sim N\big(Z_o b_0,\ \Sigma_{oo}\big), \qquad \Sigma_{oo} = \Sigma_t[t_o, t_o] \circ \Sigma_s[a_o, a_o] + Z_o B Z_o^\top + \sigma_n^2 I,

where a_o and t_o are the observed cells’ areas and time steps and \circ is the elementwise product. The fixed effects are integrated out too (the Z_o B Z_o^\top term) and drawn afterwards from their exact conditional distribution. The spatial block \Sigma_s[a_o, a_o] comes from a single eigendecomposition of R, done once when the frame is built, so a change of \tau or \rho_s only rescales eigenvalues.

The MCMC therefore works on n latent values, not m \times T, and its cost per iteration grows as n^3, independently of the size of the full table. This is what makes continental maps over decades, at monthly resolution, feasible.

The sampler

Each iteration updates the latent values, then the hyperparameters.

  • Latent values by elliptical slice sampling (Murray, Adams & MacKay, 2010) against a posterior-scaled Gaussian (Nishihara, Murray & Adams, 2014): the Gaussian prior combined with a Gaussian approximation of each cell’s likelihood (pseudo-data), with the approximation divided back out, so the update is exact. Proposing on this ellipse, rather than the prior’s, is what lets heavily surveyed cells mix.
  • Hyperparameters by two adaptive Metropolis moves: a centred move (\theta given x_o) and the surrogate-data move of Murray and Adams (2010), in which x_o moves with \theta. The centred move alone gets stuck, because n latent values pin \theta.
  • During burn-in the proposals adapt, and the pseudo-data are refitted twice to a Gaussian approximation of the likelihood at the chain’s mean latent values. Both are then fixed, so the draws after burn-in come from an exact MCMC. The refit matters most for rare outcomes, where many cells have no positives.
  • Chains start from dispersed points and run in parallel; diagnose() checks R-hat and effective sample sizes of every parameter, the latent value of every observed cell included.

Prediction and aggregation

For each posterior draw of (\theta, \beta, x_o), the full m \times T surface is drawn by conditional simulation (Matheron’s rule): an unconditional draw of the field, corrected by kriging so that it agrees with x_o. This is exact, and needs no matrix larger than n \times n beyond the stored eigenvectors; the work is split into blocks of areas so that memory stays bounded.

Each draw of the surface is then aggregated to any grouping of the areas (regions, countries) as a weighted mean, and only then summarised. Group estimates therefore carry the correlation between their areas, which averaging area-level summaries would lose.

Cross-validation

crossval() holds out folds of observed cells, refits, and predicts each held-out cell from its exact conditional distribution given the fitted cells, nugget included. The log predictive density integrates that Gaussian against the binomial likelihood by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature, and calibration is checked with a randomised probability integral transform.

Scale

Two things set the cost of a fit:

  • The eigendecomposition of the graph. areal_frame() does it once. It is a dense m \times m problem, costing O(m^3) in the number of areas m: quick for hundreds of areas, noticeably slower for thousands. Build the frame once and save it with saveRDS().
  • Each MCMC iteration. It costs O(n^3) in the number of observed cells n, because of a dense Cholesky factorisation. It does not depend on the number of areas or time steps.

The sampler is almost entirely dense linear algebra, so an optimised BLAS (Intel MKL, OpenBLAS or Apple Accelerate) makes a large difference over R’s reference BLAS. The method was developed on about 1,300 and 1,800 observed cells. Prediction holds one block of areas at a time, so memory stays bounded however many draws are used.
